articles.text: Are your kids asking for a smartphone, smartwatch or iPad for the holidays? If you’re feeling hesitant, you’re not alone. According to Common Sense Media, one in four kids has their own cellphone by age 8. Giving a child a smartphone means more than buying a phone: it opens the door to unrestricted web access, algorithmically targeted advertising, and intense social pressures from online peer networks, long before their brains are ready to manage it. At Piedmont Unplugged, we advocate waiting until high school for smartphone ownership and age 16 for social media use. Delaying both gives kids a balanced childhood and time to develop the social, emotional, and cognitive skills they need for healthy adolescence and adulthood. To help your family navigate the holiday tech pressure, here’s a framework for being intentional about when, what, and how. Step 1: Clarify your purpose Before choosing a device, identify the needs you’re trying to meet. For example: 1. Coordination and Safety: Knowing when soccer practice ends or when they’re walking home from school. 2. Social Belonging: Helping them coordinate their own playdates and stay in touch with friends. 3. Entertainment: A useful tool for travel or downtime. Landlines, flip phones, and trusted neighbors can meet essential communication and safety needs without a web browser or app store. When my elementary school-aged sons walk around the neighborhood, they know they can ask a friendly neighbor to “call mom.” Going without live GPS tracking has helped them build real-world confidence, problem-solving skills, situational awareness, and a stronger sense of community. Step 2: Evaluate signs of readiness Maturity matters more than age. Ask yourself: 1. Screen transitions: After a five-minute warning, can they stop watching TV or playing a video game calmly, or does it trigger an instant meltdown? 2. Real-world conflict: Can they read social cues and work through playground disagreements face-to-face? 3. Boredom and offline habits: Do they spend free afternoons biking, playing, or doing other activities, or do they usually ask for a device when bored? 4. Accountability: Are they truthful and able to discuss rules? If your child struggles to stop playing a video game, the endless scroll of TikTok or Instagram poses an even greater challenge for their developing brains. Our goal is to raise kids who have the social-emotional awareness to be kind, the skills to self-regulate, and the confidence to navigate the world without relying on a device. Step 3: Assess your own readiness and bandwidth Ask whether you have the time and energy for: 1. Setting up and monitoring parental controls. 2. Establishing clear house rules through a family media plan. 3. Discussing digital boundaries and online safety regularly. Educating and setting boundaries now can protect your peace of mind and your child’s well-being. Together, we can create an environment where our kids don’t need a smartphone to feel connected. articles.text: With more rain forecast this week and a potentially historic El Niño expected this winter, now is the time to protect your home from flooding and prepare for power outages. The city recommends that residents not wait until heavy rains begin to learn if their home is vulnerable to flooding. If your home has a sump pump, checking it should be your priority. Sump pumps wear out over time, and many homeowners don’t discover theirs has stopped working until the basement floods. Test your pump now to make sure it’s working properly and has a backup power source. If you don’t know how to test your sump pump, call a plumber now to have it inspected. Identify and address drainage problems now to reduce the risk of flooding again. Other steps to take before heavy rain arrives: • Clear gutters and drains. Remove leaves and debris from gutters, downspouts, basement drains, and drainage Public Works employees fill sandbags at the Corporation Yard for residents to take home and use to protect against flooding. Piedmont residents can get 10 free sandbags per household at the City’s Corporation Yard (898 Red Rock Road) Monday-Friday, 7 a.m.-3:30 p.m. Document your home and belongings. Take photos of each room and valuable belongings if you need to file an insurance claim. Intense storms can bring down trees and power lines, causing outages that last for hours or even days. Make a plan now for how your household would manage an extended outage. Consider whether you would be able to stay in your home without power for several days. articles.text: A feature film made for $200,000 by Piedmont residents Kevin and Karyn Yarris has won Best Feature Film at the City of Angels Film Festival. Their romantic drama, I’ve Got You, follows two estranged brothers brought back to their childhood family home after losing their sibling. One brother battles addiction, the other rediscovers love and purpose. The couple shot the film in just 18 days. An exploration of grief, redemption, and family bonds, I’ve Got You premiered at the Catalina Film Festival in September and has received eight festival nominations. The filmmakers have deep Piedmont roots. Karyn grew up in the city and graduated from Piedmont High School before studying drama at the National Conservatory of Dramatic Arts. She began as an actor but found she preferred working behind the scenes, eventually becoming a full-time producer. Karyn’s producer credits include feature films No Evidence of Man and Deer Season. Kevin was born in Oakland and raised in Piedmont, where his family was close to Karyn’s. The two reconnected years later and married in 2017. Kevin began screenwriting after Karyn asked him to revise a bank-heist script. He substantially rewrote it, and the couple sold it to a company that made it into the film Blowback. They then turned to a script that Karyn had optioned some 20 years earlier from Greg Stechman, a screenwriter and director who previously worked with Karyn on the 2008 thriller Anxiety. “The original script was very depressing, but it had some beautiful, emotional content in it,” Kevin remembered. He went to work and rewrote the 120-page script, preserving its emotional core. The couple then produced the film through their company, Wildwood Entertainment Inc. They enlisted their longtime friend Joshua B. Porter, a director experienced in low-budget filmmaking, to direct and co-produce. Casting took six months and involved thousands of auditions and chemistry reads. The film stars Aaron Dominguez (Only Murders in the Building) as Tyler, Nicholas Cirillo (Outer Banks) as Kyle, and Madeline Popovich (One Summer) as Maddy. The Yarrises filmed in Calaveras County, where their cabins and those of family friends served as both locations and lodging. That helped keep costs down during the 18-day shoot in fall 2025. The couple also handled lodging, payroll, and on-set rewrites, and even cooked breakfast for the crew. “You’re putting out fires and making sure that everyone has what they need, and the actors are taken care of,” said Karyn. Since its September 2026 premiere at Catalina, I’ve Got You has screened at the Show Low Film Festival, City of Angels Film Festival, Rehoboth Beach International Film Festival and FirstGlance Hollywood Film Festival. Their romantic drama, I’ve Got You, follows two estranged brothers brought back to their childhood family home after losing their sibling. One brother battles addiction, the other rediscovers love and purpose. The couple shot the film in just 18 days. An exploration of grief, redemption, and family bonds, I’ve Got You premiered at the Catalina Film Festival in September and has received eight festival nominations. The filmmakers have deep Piedmont roots. Karyn grew up in the city and graduated from Piedmont High School before studying drama at the National Conservatory of Dramatic Arts. She began as an actor but found she preferred working behind the scenes, eventually becoming a full-time producer. Karyn’s producer credits include feature films No Evidence of Man and Deer Season. Kevin was born in Oakland and raised in Piedmont, where his family was close to Karyn’s. The two reconnected years later and married in 2017. Kevin began screenwriting after Karyn asked him to revise a bank-heist script. He substantially rewrote it, and the couple sold it to a company that made it into the film Blowback. They then turned to a script that Karyn had optioned some 20 years earlier from Greg Stechman, a screenwriter and director who previously worked with Karyn on the 2008 thriller Anxiety. “The original script was very depressing, but it had some beautiful, emotional content in it,” Kevin remembered. articles.text: Teachers in red union shirts stood behind Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) Co-President Sam Colburn as he raised concerns about the proposed changes to Piedmont’s math pathways at the October 14 school board meeting. “All process has been eroded or expunged from this school district when it comes to course adoption,” said Colburn during the meeting. The Piedmont Unified School District board approved the new pathways later that evening with implementation planned for the next school year. The Board also directed Assistant Superintendent Dolowich to establish a math committee where the district could collaborate with math teachers on specific parameters. Parameters to be collaborated on include curriculum adoption, refinements of approved math pathways, a math placement policy including assessments, clarity on standards covered in each course and a transition plan for implementation. The district will provide an update to the community once all items are completed. “Thus far, collaboration with the Math Committee has been very positive and, ultimately, clarity on [parameters] will be reached through this process,” said Dolowich. The district does not plan any tracking for the sixth or seventh grade courses, and expects to hire math teachers to provide targeted intervention and enrichment for the 6th and 7th grade math courses. One of the district’s goals is to make Algebra 1 accessible by eighth grade. “In disaggregating the data, mixed student results were evident for specific groups, such as non-compression students in grades 6 & 7 and Math Lab class results. These were two of a number of reasons cited by the district on Oct. 14th for the changes,” Dolowich told the Post. “The construct of the current math pathway is ten years old and in moving forward we will have the ability to adopt a new, more advantageous curriculum for our students. Students will be afforded a clear progression that assesses readiness earlier and offers more flexibility, and includes additional support in the earlier grades, at grade 6 and in pre-algebra,” said Dolowich. The district agrees that there needs to be clarity on standards covered in each course. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich met with math teachers the last week of October and believes important progress and collaboration has been made towards a common ground. At the high school level, the district plans to phase out integrated math in favor of a sequence of Algebra 1, Geometry and Algebra 2. Karna Sacchi, the parent of a recent Piedmont High School graduate welcomes the change away from the current Integrated Math (IM) sequence. “For my son, repeated superficial coverage of topics left him feeling like he never really understood them as compared to the in-depth coverage of topics in Honors Math Analysis (non-IM). His math tutor had seen the same thing with his other students whose schools used an IM curriculum,” said Sacchi. But the middle school changes have drawn objections from teachers concerned about how quickly students will progress. The Post asked veteran middle school math teacher Karen Bloom, who teaches non-compression math 7 and 8, whether additional teaching support would make a common sixthgrade pathway workable. “I do not think adding a second math teacher will allow all students to access the curriculum faster than the 6th grade curriculum currently requires,” said Bloom. “It will certainly help us differentiate more for students, but that doesn’t mean they all will be able to learn more quickly than their developmental level allows.” Bloom also expressed concern that some students are still catching up from pandemic-era distance learning. “There are still a number of students who still do not understand fractions and decimals when they come to middle school,” she said. The district also aims to make advanced math, including calculus, more accessible in high school. When asked whether reaching Calculus BC should be a goal for every student, Bloom disagreed. “I do not think this should be a goal for all students. I don’t believe in the race to nowhere. Students should work at age and grade appropriate levels and go deep on their understanding rather than going fast and gaining only shallow conceptual understanding,” said Bloom. “There is no reason to go faster. It would be better to go deeper.” The math committee has until May 26 to finalize their formal recommendation to adopt next year’s math pathways and curriculum. A change is already approved, but details of the pathways, curriculum adoption, and the transition implementation plan are in process of being ironed out with staff to best set students up for success.

articles.text: Lila Staley, a Beach School 3rd grader, is the 2026 winner of the Giant Jack weight-guessing competition, winning possession of the Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch’s centerpiece for Halloween. Her guess of 739.52 pounds was just 2.48 pounds off the actual 742-pound weigh-in for the Giant pumpkin. Staley’s prognostication was the closest out of 313 guesses the patch received during their annual fundraiser. The pumpkin was delivered to her family on October 30. “The win came as a complete surprise but was a super cool thing to have at the house for Halloween,” said Staley. “So many neighbors and friends were asking about and since we live on Oakland Avenue it had a lot of visibility. Staley submitted her guess at the same time as her mother and sister, who guessed 900 and 1000 pounds, respectively. Guesses collected by Pumpkin Patch volunteers ranged from 100 to 9,000 pounds. articles.text: The wait for Neverland is almost over as Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class will present Peter Pan and Wendy by Lauren Gunderson Thursday-Saturday, November 12-14. This charming, empowering reimagination of J.M. Barrie’s classic Peter Pan follows Wendy Darling, played by junior Lucy Shoop, after just finding out her parents are sending her to finishing school. “There is so much about Lauren Gunderson’s adaptation to be excited about. She has taken the original play by J.M. Barrie and updated its themes and plot. Though Pan still brings Wendy to Neverland to be a mother, Wendy wants instead to be a scientist, idolizing Marie Curie,” said play director Kim Taylor. Peter Pan, played by junior Miles Simon, still doesn’t want to grow up but he does gain some emotional maturity throughout the course of the play. The cast includes Joshua Bell, Ida Bertsch-Marshall, Quinton Cole, Savannah Dennig, Yiyou Fang, Ethan Hammond, Jack Herrlinger, Stella Joseph, Zayd Mahmood, Eli Mittan, Rowan Murphy, Sophia Puckett, Dresden Schulte Sasse, Lucy Shoop, Miles Simon, Leela Sivakumar, Aliana Tejeda, Lukas Toth, Lauren Udovch, Grette Willats, and Riley Wood. “This production has a bit of everything — aerial tricks, sword fighting, a couple of songs, and lots of heart. We’ve had a great time rehearsing it, and we’re so happy to share it with the community,” said Taylor. “The play teaches the audience to enhance their imagination and to not give up on their aspirations. Anything is possible if you put your mind to it,” said Sophia Puckett, who plays the pirate Smee. All shows are at Alan Harvey Theatre at Piedmont High School, 800 Magnolia Avenue. Tickets are all reserved seats and can be purchased at phsacting.ludus.com. Tickets are $12 for students and $20 for general admission. PEF’s Community Engagement Committee invites the masses to come enjoy free beverages, light bites and lively conversation. Some site principals, teachers, as well as school and community leaders will be present. The play is approximately two hours in length, and is suitable for ages seven and up. articles.text: During November and December, Chabot Space & Science Center continues its mission to make science and space education accessible for learners of all ages. For communities across Oakland, the East Bay, and beyond, Chabot offers hands-on opportunities that strengthen real-world skills, support connection, and help participants see themselves in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Chabot’s Science Instructors are developing new programming, the in-house exhibits team continues to expand interactive learning spaces, and volunteers are ready to welcome visitors, both in the Center and while exploring the night sky. Astrophotography 101 returns: skills you can use in the real world On November 19, Chabot will bring back Astrophotography 101 workshops, building on the excitement generated by their Shared Sky exhibition. Partnering with CDARC, Chabot will host workshops focused on practical techniques for capturing astronomical objects, including both equipment uses and final image processing. Instructors guide learners through the full workflow, including using equipment to capture targets in the sky, setting up and refining observational techniques and processing images to produce a polished final result. For those seeking inspiration before attending, Chabot recommends visiting Shared Sky: Photos of Our Universe. Their newest exhibition showcases astrophotography by Bay Area photographers and by global winners of the 2026 Astrophotography Prize, along with images taken by Hubble and Webb (and soon to come Roman). The message is clear: astrophotography is both a scientific practice and a creative pathway. The astrophotography series continues in the coming months with Milky Way Astrophotography on January 21 and Astrophotography with a Star Tracker on February 11. Family astronomy and group learning opportunities Chabot also brings back Family Astronomy, an excellent way for families, student groups, and community organizations to learn together. These sessions support shared exploration by encouraging questions, strengthening science knowledge, and promoting hands-on engagement. Whether attendees are experienced skywatchers or complete beginners, the program is designed for accessible learning for all ages! The Geminids Meteor Shower: a community viewing experience From December 13–14, Chabot will highlight one of the most spectacular night-sky events of the year: the Geminids Meteor Shower. articles.text: It was a historic Saturday, November 7 for the Piedmont High girls’ volleyball team. With a come-from-behind 3-2 victory over No. 5 San Domenico as the No. 3 seeded school in the Division 3 bracket, the Highlanders captured the school’s first-ever North Coast Section title. It marked the school’s third NCS championship appearance after reaching the finals in 2008 and 1999, but they never won it until that Saturday evening in Binks Rawlings Gym. “This team knows they’ve had the potential all year. It was great to see them do it and close against a great team, I’m super happy for them,” co-head coach Mike Glass said. The girls’ volleyball team’s ascent over the last few years has been somewhat of a surprise. Piedmont went 3-19 in 2024 before jumping to 9-12 in 2025, achieving their first NCS berth since 2018. articles.text: Emma Chan, Faith Chin reach doubles final It was a mightily successful Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament for Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team on Friday and Saturday, November 6-7. Sophomore Ella Ruthven came away with this year’s singles title, while the senior duo of Emma Chan and Faith Chin finished as runners up in the doubles bracket. In the singles final, Ruthven won in three sets after dropping the first in a 2-6, 6-1, 6-4 victory over Bishop O’Dowd’s Ellena Kau. Ruthven entered as the No. 1 seed, opening with a 6-0, 6-1 win over Berkeley’s Cambria Frozena. In the quarterfinals she shut out Castro Valley’s Claire Liu 6-0, 6-0, and swept Piedmont teammate Maddy Huynh 6-0, 6-0 in the semifinals. “In the first set, I was hitting my shots too short and she was able to take advantage of that. I changed my mindset, and I started hitting the ball deeper and heavier; that kind of threw her off her game. I may have been a little nervous in the first set and maybe stopped moving my feet a bit. In the second set, I was really determined to come back, so I started improving my feet and my shots.” Ruthven said of her finals win. As for Chan and Chin, Emma’s finals appearance in the doubles bracket marked her second consecutive after winning last year’s title alongside former teammate Samantha Huynh. “It’s very surprising. I never really expect to get to the final and just take things match by match. But, I’m happy to get this far and be able to play with Faith, that was really fun for us,” Chan said. Chan and Chin entered as the top seed in the tournament. They beat Berkeley’s Rowan and Charlotte Crawley 6-0, 6-0 in the first round, won 6-1, 6-1 over O’Dowd’s Vivienne Manning and Avani Shah in the quarterfinals, and beat Alameda’s Naomi Lin and Carolina Sue 6-4, 6-1 Staff Photos Ella Ruthven (left) stands with the first-place medal for the WACC Individual Tournament’s singles’ bracket alongside finalist, Bishop O’Dowd’s Ellen in the semifinals. They ran into O’Dowd’s Ayla Akcaoglu and Edie Kevanie in the finals, losing 6-1, 6-3. “You’d think Faith and my connection would be a bit iffy because she’s been a singles player all three years on varsity, while I played doubles consistently. But we clicked nicely. We found our footing quickly, so we were really in sync. We did a lot of poaching. Faith poached a lot of shots and I tried to overhead or volley when I could. That really helped speed things up,” Chan said. “Emma and I played together freshman year, so we already had some chemistry and knowledge of our games. We practiced a bit the last two weeks together and communicated really well. We had a slow start [in the semifinals], and tried to out-rally them, but we switched it up to get them in difficult positions,” Chin mentioned. Huynh, a freshman, finished third in the singles bracket after entering as the fourth seed. She won 6-0, 6-1 over Berkeley’s Franny Bertolini in the first round, and then beat Alameda’s Lucille Clasen 6-3, 6-0 in the second round. After falling to Ruthven in the semis, she beat Alameda’s Natalie Wong 6-3, 7-6 (7-3) in the third-place final. Other results Chiara Silvio and Mai Pham won the consolation bracket’s doubles title, winning 8-6 over Alameda’s Morgan Takada and Nora Lloyd. After losing in the first-round to O’Dowd’s Fiona Wood and Sloane Kah by narrow scores of 7-6 (7-5), 7-6 (7-5), they followed up with an 8-2 win over Berkeley’s Cif Frydman and Ceci Grant in the consolation firstround, and won 8-3 over CV’s Kaylee Cheng and Kaylee Ly in the semifinals. Leela Sivakumar reached the consolation bracket’s singles finals, losing 8-2 to O’Dowd Ella Sims. She lost to Wong 6-1, 6-2 in the opening round, but followed up with an 8-2 win over CV’s Hailey Marsh to start the consolation bracket, and then beat Berkeley Erin Lao 8-1 in the consolation semifinals. Amelia Oldrin and Amalia Angulo lost to O’Dowd’s Manning and Shah in three sets in the first round, 6-3, 3-6, 10-7. They beat Berkeley’s Marilyn Whiteside and Isa Bijl-Thompson 9-8 (7-4) in the consolation first round, but fell 8-1 to Takao and Lloyd in the semifinals. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team’s season concluded in the first round of the Division 1 North Coast Section playoffs, losing to top-seed Northgate 15-6 while playing at Campolindo in Moraga on Thursday, November 5. Regardless of the result, it marked the first time the Highlanders competed in Div.1, the top bracket. “It’s a huge accomplishment to get to Division 1, we’ll take that. This is great, competition and I’m super proud of what we accomplished throughout the season. It says we’re working hard and have a lot of heart,” said PHS coach Rik Krumins. Their D1 berth marked a one-ranking improvement over last year’s top seed in the DIC. 2 ladder, despite losing several key seniors from 2025. “When I saw the bracket, I was stoked. We are built with sophomores and juniors, and showed a lot of progress. This was our first year in D1, and we’re going to come back next year and win more games,” said junior Henry Stein said. “We came into D1, and rather than being stars struck, we were aggressive and went at it. We played mature against a No. 1 seed, and put up a good fight. No one expected us to do this well, and we scored six,” added junior Rylan Patty. The future looks bright for the program in 2027 with Stein, Patty, and sophomore goalie Dylan Jerez leading the charge. “Working on the fundamentals was a big part of our game because we’re young. Everyone showed a lot of growth, especially with passing and shooting. Just talking to Walker [Wilson], he dapped me up and said, ‘I’m not too sad about this season.’ We have so much to look forward to next season,” Patty said. “I felt confident. I didn’t play my best game and feel I could’ve kept it a lot closer. Next year, we’re going to have Ben [Kappes] and Ben’s little brother. A lot of the guys are playing club, so we’re going to be really deep,” Jerez said. Only two seniors graduate with this year’s class, key players Stein, Patty, Jerez, Henry Van Den Bos, Graham Smith, Walker Wilson, Oliver Hurwitz, and Ben Kappesr. “We’re not losing anybody. We’re going to build off this going into the offseason. We want Staff Photos Henry Stein scored three goals in Piedmont’s loss to D1 top-seed Northgate. Rylan Patty scored twice against Northgate. to hit the pool next fall and expect big things,” Stein said. Match Recap Northgate opened with the game’s first two goals to go up 2-0 at the 5:12 mark. Thirty seconds later, PHS got on the board when Van Den Bos scored their first goal. The Broncos notched the next three goals to lead 5-1 with 2:30 left. Patty got one back with 30 seconds left, making it a 5-2 deficit going into the second. From there, Northgate scored the first two goals of the second quarter to lead 7-2 with 4:14 remaining. Patty scored again with 3:17 left, cutting it to 7-3, but the Broncos scored another pair of goals to lead 9-3 with 1:14 on the clock. Stein scored Piedmont’s fourth with 45 seconds left in the half. In the third quarter, Northgate scored another pair to push its lead to 11-4 after a minute and a half. Stein scored another with 4:39 to go, but Northgate answered quickly 17 seconds later on its next possession ad bagged one more with 41 seconds left. Northgate made it 14-5 with 5:43 left, while Stein scored PHS’ final goal 30 seconds later. The Broncos notched theirs final goal with 3:33 remaining. Final scorers: Stein scored three goals, Patty had two, and Van Den Bos had one. Goalie Dylan Jerez is one of Piedmont’s returners for 2027, which could potentially be a strong roster and NCS contenders.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s football season came to an end on Friday, November 6, finishing their campaign with a one-sided 33-0 shutout of Alameda on the Hornets’ home field. We came in with the mentality that this was do or die, and point differential would play a factor, so we never took our foot off the gas,” senior linebacker Colby Hong said. Friday’s result was one of Piedmont’s best of the season. Their defense got after the quarterback all night, making life a nightmare for the Hornets’ offense. “Throughout the season, we got in a better mentality of just needing to win. articles.text: Photo by Kevin Berne Katie Lowes in the West Coast premiere of Liberation. Berkeley Repertory Theatre is presenting Liberation, a play by Bess Wohl that examines the women’s liberation movement of the 1970s, now through November 29. The West Coast premiere, directed by Tony Award nominee Whitney White, runs through Nov. 29 at Berkeley Rep’s Roda Theatre. The play received the 2026 Pulitzer Prize for Drama and Tony Award for Best Play following its Broadway run. Set in 1970s Ohio, the play follows Lizzie, who brings together a group of women in a recreation center basement to discuss their lives and work toward social change. Decades later, Lizzie’s daughter explores her mother’s history, revisiting the group’s discussions and examining questions about women’s freedom and equality. The production moves between the two generations, exploring the relationship between the feminist movement’s original goals and the questions that remain unresolved. “Berkeley has a very special relationship to the history of the women’s movement, having fostered and produced many champions of women’s rights who laid the foundations of the movement and continue to push us forward today,” White said in a press release. “Liberation was a labor of love and resistance, and I cannot wait for audiences to meet these unforgettable characters.” The cast includes Katie Lowes as Lizzie, Felicia Curry as Celeste, Britt Faulkner as Dora, Irene Sofia Lucio as Isidora, Gunnar Manchester as Bill, Mary Gordon Murray as Margie, Veronica Otim as Joanna and Evelyn Spahr as Susan. articles.text: Shotgun Players is streaming The Fall Show, a surreal romance story of older love based on the works of playwright Charles Mee, now through Monday, November 16. The Fall Show features main characters Eddie and Sam, who are joined by a six-person ensemble that serves to disrupt and evoke the ups and downs of falling in love. Mee was an American playwright, historian and author known for experimental plays that combined classical literature, historical texts, popular culture and contemporary themes. His best-known plays include Big Love, a contemporary adaptation of the Greek tragedy The Suppliants; bobrauschenbergamerica, inspired by the collage art of Robert Rauschenberg; Orestes 2.0 and The Trojan Women: A Love Story, modern adaptations of Greek tragedies; and Hotel Cassiopeia, about artist Joseph Cornell. The Fall Show is directed and choreographed by Erika Chong Shuch. In a press release, director Shuch said she and dramaturg Sarah Rose Leonard “combed the expanse of Charles Mee’s corpus of plays for a story that resonated.” “I’ve been thinking about how the love stories of middle-aged and older adults­ — and I include myself in this category — are muted. Falling in love, being in love, maintaining love: it’s complicated, twisty, chaotic,” said Shuch. “I hope I continue to be baffled by how to love, because it means I’m still thinking about it, still trying for it, still rooting for it, still valuing it.” The play received positive reviews and was extended through November 1 following its premiere in October. articles.text: Ha Chong-Hyun The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco presents the first major North American museum retrospective of Korean contemporary artist Ha Chong-Hyun, featuring more than 50 paintings spanning more than six decades. Ha Chong-Hyun: Retrospective is on view now through January 25, 2027, and includes works dating from the early 1960s through 2025, including two paintings completed last year. Seoul-based scholar and curator Sunjung Kim is the guest curator. Born in 1935 during Japanese colonial rule, Ha developed his artistic practice in the aftermath of the Korean War. The political and economic conditions of postwar South Korea influenced his work, including his use of industrial burlap sacks once used to transport rice into the country. Ha began experimenting with unconventional painting techniques in the 1960s, layering thick paint onto canvas, embedding thread into surfaces and using fire to alter materials. His later White Paper on Urban Planning series reflected South Korea’s rapid industrialization through geometric grids and radiating lines. A founding member of the Korean Avant-Garde Association in 1969, Ha also addressed the political restrictions of the period. His 1971 work Counter-Phase incorporates stacks of censored newspapers and blank pages. Ha’s best-known series, Conjunction, began in 1974 and introduced his signature “back-pressure” technique. He applies thick oil paint to the reverse of burlap canvas, pressing it through the fabric’s coarse weave to create textured surfaces. “For Ha, painting is not about illusion or representation,” Kim said. “It is about the encounter — between the artist’s body and the material, between pressure and release. That encounter is what gives the work its enduring power.” Associated with South Korea’s Dansaekhwa, or monochrome painting movement, Ha shares its emphasis on repetition and restrained palettes but is distinguished by his physical approach to materials. In the 2010s, he began incorporating brighter primary colors. His recent work also combines paint with charred materials and ash. Visit https://exhibitions.asian art.org/exhibitions/ha-chonghyun-retrospective/ to learn more.

articles.text: Ukulele virtuoso Jake Shimabukuro returns to San Francisco’s Miner Auditorium Dec. 3-6 with a holiday-themed program featuring seasonal favorites and his signature blend of musical styles. Born and raised in Honolulu, Hawai‘i, Shimabukuro began playing the ukulele at age 4. He first gained international recognition with a viral rendition of George Harrison’s While My Guitar Gently Weeps, which introduced millions of viewers to the instrument. Often called the “Jimi Hendrix of the ukulele,” Shimabukuro has built an international following for his ability to incorporate elements of jazz, rock, classical, blues, folk and traditional Hawaiian music into his performances. His playing pushes beyond the ukulele’s traditional sound, producing everything from rock-inspired arrangements to jazz standards and original compositions. Since his 2002 debut album Sunday Morning, Shimabukuro has released 25 albums for English- and Japanese-speaking markets. His 2006 recording of Gently Weeps helped establish his popularity in the United States, while his 2012 album Grand Ukulele, produced by Alan Parsons, further showcased his technical range. He has also collaborated with artists including Bette Midler, Yo-Yo Ma, Jimmy Buffett, Ziggy Marley and Mick Fleetwood. For his SFJAZZ performances, Shimabukuro will perform holiday classics with a Polynesian influence. The program will feature Shimabukuro on ukulele, accompanied by a bassist. SFJAZZ hosts performances Thursday, Dec. 3, Friday, Dec. 4, and Saturday, Dec. 5, at 7:30 p.m., and Sunday, Dec. 6, at 3 p.m. All performances are at Miner Auditorium, 201 Franklin St. in San Francisco. Tickets range from $45 to $140, depending on the performance and seating. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/26-27/jakeshimabukuro/ to purchase tickets. Jake Shimabukuro

articles.text: Internationally acclaimed soprano Lise Davidsen returns to Cal Performances for a recital at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall November 19, performing a program that combines classical art songs with traditional Christmas music. The recital brings together the German art song tradition and seasonal music, offering audiences a program that spans classical repertoire and familiar holiday selections. Accompanied by pianist James Baillieu, Davidsen will perform works by Johann Sebastian Bach, Max Reger and Richard Strauss, as well as Richard Wagner’s Wesendonck Lieder, a song cycle influenced by the composer’s opera Tristan und Isolde. The program concludes with traditional Christmas favorites sung in English, German, Italian and Norwegian. Davidsen, a native of Norway, has earned international recognition for her powerful voice and performances on major opera stages. She recently appeared as Lady Macbeth in the Metropolitan Opera’s production of Verdi’s Macbeth. Concert begins at 7:30 p.m. Visit https://calperformances.org/ to purchase tickets. articles.text: Haus Alpenz and the extraordinary world of oxidative wines Rancio Sec: The taste of the sun In an age obsessed with freshness, immediacy and youthful fruit, American importer Haus Alpenz is making a compelling case for some of the wine world’s most historic and misunderstood treasures. From the sun-drenched terraces of Roussillon to the Atlantic island of Madeira, these are wines shaped by patience, oxygen and the passage of time. There are few more fascinating expressions of wine than those in which time itself becomes an ingredient. Long before the modern obsession with pristine fruit, reductive winemaking and youthful freshness, winemakers across the Mediterranean were producing wines that embraced oxygen, warmth and extended maturation. The results were complex, often extraordinary, and sometimes capable of surviving for generations. Today, much of this tradition survives in a handful of historic wine regions. Through its specialist Sotolon Selections portfolio, American importer Haus Alpenz has brought together an exceptional collection of these wines, championing producers whose work preserves an important but frequently overlooked part of European wine culture. At the center of this collection are the Rancio Sec wines of Roussillon, the Vin Doux Naturels of Maury, Rivesaltes and Banyuls, and the remarkable fortified wines of Madeira. I recently had the opportunity to attend a tasting of the Haus Alpenz portfolio conducted by their national sales manager, Jake Parrott. He is a warm, jovial fellow with an encyclopedic knowledge of these obscure wines and even though I have been writing about wine for 25 years, there was so much I learned from the tasting. Perhaps the most intriguing category is Rancio Sec, a dry oxidative wine with deep roots in Catalan winemaking tradition. Produced on both sides of the French-Spanish border, these wines are increasingly rare, representing an almost forgotten approach to maturation. Unlike conventional wines, Rancio Sec is deliberately exposed to oxygen over extended periods, often in partially filled old oak barrels. Some producers also expose their wines to outdoor conditions, allowing temperature fluctuations and the Mediterranean climate to contribute to their development. The resulting wines are extraordinary. Walnut, roasted almond, dried citrus, tobacco, cocoa and exotic spices combine with savory, sometimes saline characteristics. There is often an unmistakable impression of the Mediterranean landscape: Domaine de Sau’s Rivesaltes Rancio was my favorite wine of the tasting. There is often an unmistakable impression of the Mediterranean landscape: Jake Parrott of Haus Alpenz shows off his tasting lineup sun-warmed stone, dried herbs and the sea. These are wines that challenge conventional tasting expectations and reward an open mind. Maury and Rivesaltes: The legacy of Grenache Further inland, the appellations of Maury and Rivesaltes represent another extraordinary chapter in Roussillon’s wine history. Here, Grenache is central to the story. The region’s intense Mediterranean sunshine produces grapes of remarkable ripeness and concentration, while the traditional addition of grape spirit during fermentation preserves natural sweetness and creates the Vin Doux Naturel style. In Maury, the wines can be intensely expressive, combining dark cherry, blackberry and plum with chocolate, coffee and spice. Younger examples possess considerable richness, while older wines develop extraordinary tertiary complexity. Producers such as Domaine du Dernier Bastion and Mas Peyre demonstrate the diversity of the appellation, including the fascinating Rancio expressions that develop through prolonged oxidative ageing. Rivesaltes, meanwhile, offers an extraordinary spectrum of styles and ages. articles.text: Last Wednesday the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a good turnout of 42 walkers and five K-9 best friends at the Exedra for their weekly walk. The group was there for part two of a question Wednesday walker and local realtor Moya Robinson had posed on a September walk: “Does the architect affect the value of a home?” Moya had done more research to share, and this time she took the group to see the homes themselves. Moya said some of the notable architects who designed homes during Piedmont’s major 1907 to 1940 building period were Albert Farr, Julia Morgan, Bernard Maybeck, Charles Sumner Greene, and Newsom & Newsom. She had assumed there would be a clear premium for their homes, but when she looked at the actual sales, she didn’t find a direct correlation. There is an inherent value to the design and craftsmanship of these homes. It’s not just their names. Moya led the group up Highland Avenue to 456 Wildwood Avenue, a grand Tudor estate Albert Farr designed in 1918. It is a large home of nearly 10,000 square feet, and it sold in 2022 for $12,000,000, the highest Piedmont sale that year. Its marketing never mentioned Farr, so it was the home’s architectural quality and preservation, not the architect’s name, that carried its value. The group agreed the home was beautiful and posed for a group photo in front of its gate. Just next door was 472 Wildwood, another Albert Farr mansion, this one in the Normandy/ French Revival style and built in 1928. It has a prominent round turret, a steep roof, shutters, multi-pane windows and formal symmetrical detailing. Farr was mentioned when it sold in 2014, but the price landed in the middle of the market, so his name did not command a premium. The group continued up Wildwood to 200 Crocker Avenue, a Julia Morgan built in 1926 on a little more than half an acre. It is a grand Mediterranean with a stucco exterior, tile roof, arched openings, formal symmetrical gardens and generous indoor and outdoor spaces for entertaining. When it sold in 1999, the price was impressive for the time, but not for a house of its size, and the Morgan name did not change that. The walkers also noted that a guest house recently built next door beautifully mirrors Morgan’s design. Moya then led the group to 236 King Avenue, Unit C, a Julia Morgan Tudor built in 1915. It has steep gables, half-timbering, a brick exterior, leaded multi-pane windows and a detached carriage house and garage. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, November 11, 2026 WEDNESDAY WALKERS - MAIN Walking on Wednesday Walkers tour Piedmont homes by Farr and Morgan By Dick Carter Last Wednesday the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a good turnout of 42 walkers and five K-9 best friends at the Exedra for their weekly walk. The group was there for part two of a question Wednesday walker and local realtor Moya Robinson had posed on a September walk: “Does the architect affect the value of a home?” Moya had done more research to share, and this time she took the group to see the homes themselves. Moya said some of the notable architects who designed homes during Piedmont’s major 1907 to 1940 building period were Albert Farr, Julia Morgan, Bernard Maybeck, Charles Sumner Greene, and Newsom & Newsom. She had assumed there would be a clear premium for their homes, but when she looked at the actual sales, she didn’t find a direct correlation. There is an inherent value to the design and craftsmanship of these homes. It’s not just their names. Moya led the group up Highland Avenue to 456 Wildwood Avenue, a grand Tudor estate Albert Farr designed in 1918. It is a large home of nearly 10,000 square feet, and it sold in 2022 for $12,000,000, the highest Piedmont sale that year. Its marketing never mentioned Farr, so it was the home’s architectural quality and preservation, not the architect’s name, that carried its value. The group agreed the home was beautiful and posed for a group photo in front of its gate. Just next door was 472 Wildwood, another Albert Farr mansion, this one in the Normandy/ French Revival style and built in 1928. It has a prominent round turret, a steep roof, shutters, multi-pane windows and formal symmetrical detailing. Farr was mentioned when it sold in 2014, but the price landed in the middle of the market, so his name did not command a premium. The group continued up Wildwood to 200 Crocker Avenue, a Julia Morgan built in 1926 on a little more than half an acre. It is a grand Mediterranean with a stucco exterior, tile roof, arched openings, formal symmetrical gardens and generous indoor and outdoor spaces for entertaining. When it sold in 1999, the price was impressive for the time, but not for a house of its size, and the Morgan name did not change that. The walkers also noted that a guest house recently built next door beautifully mirrors Morgan’s design. Moya then led the group to 236 King Avenue, Unit C, a Julia Morgan Tudor built in 1915. It has steep gables, half-timbering, a brick exterior, leaded multi-pane windows and a detached carriage house and garage. In fact, the home was originally the carriage house for the 62 Farragut Avenue mansion up the street. Its timber structure and overall character remain, though the kitchen and baths are later renovations. It sold in August in a court-ordered Walkers enjoy beautiful day Route of the Walk sale because of the owner’s legal issues, well below its original asking price, so it is not a clean test of the Morgan name. The walkers continued up to 62 Farragut, the Julia Morgan Tudor Revival built at the same time as the King Avenue home. Morgan designed the mansion for James Lombard, who was educated at Harrow Public School in England and wanted his home to provide a remembrance of Harrow. It has steep gables, half-timbering, a brick base, banks of leaded windows, substantial original woodwork, arched openings and decorative ceilings. It sold in May as part of a bankruptcy proceeding, and the home needed work. For a house of its size, the price was near the bottom of the market, which shows how maintenance and the circumstances of a sale can matter as much as the architecture. Just across the street is 246 Sea View Avenue, another Julia Morgan, an English Tudor– Craftsman built in 1913. It has steep front-facing gables, stucco with dark wood half-timber detailing, deep window groupings and a strong Arts & Crafts emphasis on natural materials. The sales materials described the home like a piece of artwork, calling it a “Julia Morgan masterpiece.” When it sold in 2009, it was the most expensive home in Piedmont that year and near the top of the market for its size. It was one of the clearest examples on the tour of a home’s architectural pedigree and preservation being part of a top-ofmarket value. The last stop was up the street at 76 Sea View, an Albert Farr French Château built in 1930 with eight bedrooms. Its last listing expired in 1998 with no recorded sale, and Moya and the walkers thought it might have been sold off market. Nothing could be concluded about the Farr design’s effect on its value, but it was a wonderful home for the walkers to see. The answer to Moya’s question seemed to be yes, a famous architect could affect a home’s selling price, but maybe more important are the beauty of the design, the home’s condition, the circumstances surrounding the sale and the times. It made sense to the walkers, and the group thanked Moya for another enjoyable and informative walk. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required. Those interested should go to https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or contact the Piedmont Recreation Department at (510) 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: On Monday, November 2, the First Mondays Reading Group met to discuss their November book, The Correspondent by Virginia Evans. There was a large turnout of 28 readers for the conversation. The group was pleased to welcome Mary Prisco, who was with them for the first time. Carol Long thoughtfully dropped off snacks for the group. The Correspondent is an epistolary, a novel told through a series of written documents. It was written by American author Virginia Evans and published in 2025. Evans had previously completed seven unpublished novels, but this was her first published work. The novel started as a writing exercise and Evans had not originally planned to show it to anyone. She said it was written when she had “reached rock bottom.” Her father-in-law was sick and the country had been locked down because of Covid-19. She was 33 and on the verge of applying to law school because of the lack of success with her previous work. The novel follows the correspondence of a retired lawyer and chief legal clerk, Sybil Van Antwerp, that she sent to her friends and associates between 2012 and 2022. The novel did not receive much attention within the first few months of its being published but gradually gained popularity and reached the top of the New York Times Fiction Best Seller List on February 1, 2026. It has since received widespread praise from critics and won the 2026 Women’s Prize for Fiction. A film adaptation starring Jane Fonda was announced on March 18, 2026. The character of Sybil is based in part on Evans’ mother-in-law. Sybil is living alone in Annapolis and the divorced mother of two living adult children and one who died when he was eight. Sybil was adopted and is unsure of learning about her birth parents. She has a lifelong practice of writing letters to family members, work associates, and even famous authors. Additionally, she writes a series of unsent letters to an unknown recipient. And she is gradually losing her eyesight. Some readers were initially hesitant, maybe even reluctant, about reading the book. They wondered if a book that was so popular, and “raved” about by friends, would be really worth reading. However, like the critics, the group almost unanimously liked The Correspondent. Some readers “loved” this “wonderful” and “well crafted” book. It was “authentic” and “brilliant.” They liked the book’s style and structure and could feel the emotion in Sybil’s correspondence. It was one of those books that was hard to put down. Evans’ character development of Sybil was especially appreciated. It was noted that it is hard to really know someone. As reader Peggy Shultz had said about people, “You just don’t know.” But Sybil’s long set of writings revealed her more fully than what would have been accomplished with most authors’ descriptions of a lead character. To the surprise of some readers, they also liked this unique epistolary style. They could see Sybil’s personal evolution and understood her motivations from her letters. Some readers were initially put off by the character of Sybil. They found her to be an unpleasant, difficult person. She reminded one reader of his mother. Some readers didn’t want to read the entirety of the book because Sybil was such an unlikeable person. Other readers liked her crustiness and forthright communication. However, as her life progressed and more of her correspondence was provided, Sybil became more accessible, likeable, and understood. It was like reading her diary. There are many threads in this slow disclosure process and an intimacy with the reader developed. Aspects of some of Sybil’s relationships were “gut wrenching” for one reader. The readers wondered how Sybil’s being adopted might have affected her personality and The Correspondent by Virginia Evans desire to control her environment. She could control what was in her letters and her writing desk was like an altar. The group also considered if the death of her child made her less open but how going blind and losing control of parts of her life had the opposite effect. In her legal profession Sybil had control, order, and power too. Her job protected her. Readers asked why she would follow her lawyer partner when he became a judge and she became his clerk. It was noted that a clerkship is an important role and that the legal profession at the time was not an easy one for a woman on her own. Readers also discussed how important letters are and how writing them is becoming increasingly rare. It was said that there is “a magic with getting letters” and how much getting thank you letters, not emails or texts, from their “kids” is appreciated. (Younger readers take notice.) Readers were surprised that Evans, a young author, could present the aging process so accurately in the character of Sybil. It was also noted that good writers make readers care about the characters in their works. Evans did that for most readers. The story was not “gimmicky” or a “soap opera” for them. They cared about the people in The Correspondent. Its finest examples possess the complexity, balance and longevity to stand alongside the world’s great sweet wines. Madeira: The ultimate expression of longevity If Roussillon represents the Mediterranean tradition of oxidative ageing, Madeira is perhaps its greatest Atlantic counterpart. Produced on the volcanic Portuguese island of Madeira, these wines are defined by an extraordinary combination of acidity, fortification, oxidation and heat. Historically, the wines developed their distinctive character through prolonged exposure to warm conditions, a process that eventually became an integral part of their production. The resulting wines can be extraordinarily long-lived, retaining freshness and acidity even after many decades. Haus Alpenz represents several fascinating Madeira producers, including Belem’s, Saveiro and the historic house of Henriques & Henriques. The traditional noble varieties offer an especially compelling journey through the island’s wine culture. articles.text: • NV Tresmontaine Rancio Sec “Puits aux Souhaits” This has spent 15 years in the bottle after a long time in the solera system. It sports a nutty, smoky, pungent Oloroso-like nose that ushers in a silken-textured palate informed by toasted nuts, orange peel and a bitterness on the finish. This is both rich and bright offering a fascinating interplay of flavors. • 2002 Château de Saü Rivesaltes Rancio This enchanting wine is made from the rare Grenache Gris grape which gives it a lovely honeysuckle, jasmine floral aroma. It is similar to a dry sherry with its toasted spice, coffee, almond flavors. Medium bodied, textured and dry on the palate, it’s a beautiful wine to serve as an aperitif, or with a wide range of foods as well. Beautiful stuff. • NV Domaine Mas Blanc Banyuls “Le Colluque” Mas Blanc is one of the premier producers in Banyuls and Haus Alpenz has vintage dated bottles going back to 1947. This younger multi-vintage blend is a classic effort with its coffee, brown sugar, cassis and spicedriven aromas and flavors. Warm, mulled fruits carry over to the palate, and this medium bodied dessert wine has ample texture and a clean finish. Banyuls is known to be the perfect partner to chocolate and this example would pair wonderfully. • Saveiro Castanea Madeira 5 Year Old This gorgeous dessert wine is aged in chestnut casks which gives a perfumed floral hint to the nose. It has aromas of butterscotch, honey and English toffee. On the palate it is warm and inviting yet balanced with good acidity to keep it from being tiring. The finish is long and satisfying.
